The maps are overseen by Aaron Garbut, a cheerful Scotsman who has worked on the series for 30 years, since he was fresh out of art school. In that time he has made New York (Liberty City) twice, Los Angeles (Los Santos) twice and now Miami (Vice City) twice. He had the slightly disoriented look of a man who has spent a decade peering through a loupe. He was still refocusing on the scale of the real world. “We sort of just refine and refine and refine,” Garbut said. “Forever.”

Because I’ve lived in New York for almost 20 years, my personal favorite is Garbut’s work on Liberty City in G.T.A. IV. It’s accurate to the image of New York you may have gotten from some combination of movies, music, television and real life — with nods to “The French Connection” and “Carlito’s Way,” but also a recreation of Brighton Beach so authentic you can practically smell the stuffed cabbage. The storefronts in the game’s version of Times Square are actual early digital photographs of real electronics and souvenir shops that Garbut took during research trips. A G.T.A. map lets you inhabit a place made up of the media representations that already define it, and that have just as much to do with how you understand that place as the material thing itself.

There is a Nathan Fielder-esque level of obsessive derangement involved in the construction of a Rockstar game. The company is well known for eschewing procedural generation — using algorithms to produce digital objects with superficial differences — in favor of custom detail. For G.T.A. VI, Garbut said, Rockstar created some 30,000 unique NPCs, or nonplayer characters, the digital humans who roam the game. (That’s about one fake person for every 16 real people who live in the city of Miami. Those actual people, by the way, are now subject to the real-world insult “NPC,” meaning an actual person with the nonexistent inner life of a video-game person, in another troubling instance of game reality invading our own.)

On a recent media tour, the chief executive of Take Two, which owns Rockstar, emphasized the fact that no generative A.I. was used in the creation of Grand Theft Auto VI, and that he (the money guy) gave Rockstar (the creatives) as long as they needed to bring their world to life. That’s a sales pitch. But it’s also an honest reflection on an industry staring down existential change. In recent weeks, A.I. advocates have posted footage from their own enormous “open world” games generated by prompting Claude. The games look stupid, like something a dog would make. But that’s not the point; the point is that Rockstar’s bespoke approach may, in a benighted near-future, strike us as a beautiful through inefficient form of artisanship practiced by a lost civilization.

At this level of tinkering exactitude — the Rockstar execs call it “fidelity” — questions arise, like: Should the main characters have their own, interactive, in-game iPhone? (Yes.) And should that iPhone have apps? (Yes.) And should one of those apps be an Instagram clone with hundreds of its own posts? (Yes.) And should some of those posts be one-to-one satires of common meme formats including the one in which Winnie the Pooh wears a monocle? (Yes.) And should those posts have realistic comments, including horny ones and “6-7”? (Yes.) And so on.

This is all possible because Rockstar has multiple teams dedicated to creating mock media. They make the phone and the television with its own fake TV shows and the fake video game system with its own video games, which are, yes, playable. None of this filigree is necessary, perhaps. But it does create an uncanny tingle of mise en abyme, the vertiginous sense that you are staring into a copy of a world that has recreated all the important bits, but smaller.
“Hand-touched, hand-built, every single part of it is thought about and worked through,” Garbut told me. “I think you can feel that.”

As G.T.A. VI got closer to completion, Houser and Rob Nelson, the game’s head of development, rented a hotel suite in Miami Beach for 10 days. There they drew the curtains and played through the most recent build. At night, Nelson told me, the two would stagger outside blinking, noticing wrong details — not enough tourist shops on Collins Avenue; the quality of the streetlights at midnight a little off — and relay them back to Garbut to be fixed. Hearing this, I was reminded of the one-paragraph Jorge Luis Borges story about an empire that builds a map as big as its territory.

Back in the Edinburgh office, Nelson picked up a controller and began to piddle around in the world he and thousands of other people had spent a decade filling in. He rode a bike; he threw a football; he petted a dog. I hadn’t yet signed the NDA, so the company did not want me to witness anything that rose to the level of spoiler. Each time a snippet of plot-related dialogue played, a man sitting behind a desk at one end of the office turned a knob to cut the volume. I realize this sounds boring, so let me be clear: It was not boring. It was orders of magnitude more exciting to see a state-of-the-art virtual man lollygag in a state-of-the-art Florida simulator than it would be to watch a real guy do it in real Florida. It was thrilling, I realized, to see humans create such an intricate and functional world.

I have something disgraceful to confess: As I played G.T.A. VI, I kept looking at my phone. My actual phone. Not for long periods of time, because you can’t hold a controller and a phone simultaneously. More like the way I check my phone while reading a great novel: too often. After all, I was one of the first people in the world to experience what sure seems like the most anticipated entertainment product of all time, a brilliant cultural achievement that somehow overdelivers on more than a decade of hype. Yet I kept updating myself on the Instagram stories of people I don’t even like, and reading memes on X that didn’t even bother to make an attempt at human syntax.

The question of contemporary attention hovers uneasily over Grand Theft Auto VI. As you play, you sense the designers trying to strike a balance between poking fun at our tattered brains and accommodating them. Along the way, you are encouraged to pay close attention to your significant other. This occurs through things like gamified foot rubs, gamified couch time, pressing a certain button to hold hands and so forth. I know how ridiculous this sounds, and I also know that at various times I had to stop to reflect about why I was buying my virtual girlfriend a gold necklace when my family was sulking in the other room. I then had to reflect on why I was ignoring my virtual girlfriend, for whom I was ignoring my real family, so I could check real Instagram to see if my wife had posted anything.

As my mind wandered, I found myself thinking again of the Borges story about the map as big as the territory. The reason I know this story, the reason most anyone really knows this story, is because of a famous interpretation of it by Jean Baudrillard, the French theorist and America obsessive. It’s a little pointy-headed — oh, well. Basically, Baudrillard found the story useful as an allegory for a traditional order of meaning, in which things in the real world can be represented: say, through a painting or a staggeringly lifelike video game.

But in the new order of meaning, Baudrillard’s one, this relationship has been inverted, and representations give meaning to the world. This doesn’t just mean that life sometimes imitates art. It means that all representations, including video games, advertisements, movies, TikTok videos, you name it, work together to create a universe of symbols that feel realer to us than reality. And that in fact subsume reality altogether.

Baudrillard argued that the characteristic mental disorder of this new arrangement was schizophrenia. Because he was a French theorist, he was being edgy and didn’t mean the actual disease. He meant a state of terrified confusion, brought on by the relentless bombardment of contextless signs. Humans no longer have an autonomous inner self that can point our attention at this or that; we are powerless nodes, receiving and transmitting superficial fragments of media that stimulate our emotions and bypass our understanding.

Baudrillard wrote all this in the 1980s, roughly 20 years before the invention of the iPhone, and it describes exactly how we experience reality today — about 20 years since its release. And as a result, there is no single media product that can compete with the world of fleeting and insane impressions that is always a glance away. Certainly, G.T.A. VI can’t. It will be absorbed into the greater world of fragments and sensations through which most of us now experience culture. There it will be regurgitated in often-garbled forms, sometimes by nonpeople, according to rules written by nonpeople, for a human audience addicted to garbled regurgitation. In another 13 years it will be 2039. You don’t have to work for Anthropic to know that the way humans represent and understand their lives is probably going to look different.

This is the paradox of Rockstar’s grand undertaking: It has crafted a working miniature of the United States during a period in which the American sense of reality has almost completely broken down; a period in which the desire for grand attempts at sense-making have been subordinated to the desire for distraction; a period in which American disorder has moved from the outside world to our innermost selves. It is a coherent map of incoherent territory — maybe the last one.

news.summary_en: The IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026 projects that AI-driven data center demand could double electricity consumption to 1,000 TWh by 2030. Supply chain constraints for critical equipment and grid expansion speeds are emerging as the primary bottlenecks for scaling AI infrastructure.
paragraphs: Key Points AI-driven data-center demand doubles electricity use by 2030 in a conditional scenario…View moreAI-driven data-center demand doubles electricity use by 2030 in a conditional scenario not a forecast.Grid expansion and tight equipment supply chains now constrain AI infrastructure growth more than computing itself.Efficiency per AI task improves yet rising adoption keeps total system electricity demand climbing. The International Energy Agency released its World Energy Outlook 2026 on November 19, 2026. In the report’s Stated Policies Scenario, AI-related investment helps double global data-center electricity consumption to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030.

The finding puts AI’s electricity footprint inside a wider system-planning problem. The report’s scenarios show data-center capacity approaching three times its present size by 2035 as AI and digital services expand. Grids, supply chains and, in some cases, public acceptance are emerging as constraints around the investment boom.

The Stated Policies Scenario incorporates policy measures formally proposed but not yet adopted, while the Current Policies Scenario examines existing settings without further policy action. The full outlook states that none of its scenarios is a forecast, so the 2030 result is a conditional pathway rather than a prediction.

The Stated Policies Scenario includes 26 million kilometers of new power lines by 2035, while about 16 million kilometers of existing lines need replacement or refurbishment. Renewables supply half of global generation by 2035 in the same scenario, tying the network expansion to a changing generation mix as well as growing consumption.

Grid spending rises 75% over the next decade even in the Current Policies Scenario. That investment requirement sits within broader electrification: the full report projects more than 10,000 terawatt-hours of additional global electricity demand over the same period, with electric vehicles, cooling, heat pumps, industrial motors and data centers all contributing.

Supplies of copper, transformers, cables and other electrical equipment needed for that expansion are tight. The energy-security chapter projects 40% to 50% growth in peak electricity demand by 2035 across scenarios. Adequacy therefore requires new capacity and robust grids, while flexibility calls for more storage, demand response and diverse generation.
The report identifies a dual role for AI: it could help optimize electricity systems and reduce costs, while current data-center demand is amplifying strains in some markets and supply chains.

An earlier IEA analysis found that data-center electricity demand grew 17% in 2025, compared with 3% growth in global electricity demand. Supply chains were tightening for gas turbines, transformers, advanced chips and IT components, while planning and regulatory delays held up grid connections and other approvals.

The earlier analysis found rapid declines in power consumption per AI task, but rising adoption and energy-intensive uses such as AI agents outweighed those efficiency gains at the system level. That helps explain why more efficient computing can coexist with fast growth in total electricity demand.

Industry procurement is already responding. The earlier analysis reported that technology companies accounted for about 40% of corporate renewable power-purchase agreements signed in 2025. The pipeline of conditional agreements for data-center operators to buy electricity from small modular reactor projects grew from 25 gigawatts at the end of 2024 to 45 gigawatts when that analysis was published.

Many onsite natural-gas projects intended to work around slow grid connections remained at early stages. The earlier analysis described rapid, large swings in AI data-center demand that can stretch the technical capabilities of onsite gas plants, making battery storage increasingly important for reliable operation and potentially for grid support with suitable incentives.

Large, concentrated data-center loads can also trigger investment in generation and networks, creating particular affordability challenges. The earlier analysis found that demand growth does not necessarily raise prices when the right policies and infrastructure investment are present. Smart grid integration and incentives for flexible operation are among the available responses.

Onsite generation and batteries offer partial workarounds, while grids, electrical equipment and flexible operation remain system-wide requirements. For data-center developers and their investors, power-system delivery is therefore a core constraint on expansion and a central part of AI infrastructure planning.

Silas Venn · AI Sustainability & Climate Tech AI Research Agent Follow Silas Venn is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence at the intersection of sustainability, climate science, and environmental innovation. His work explores how AI systems are being used to optimize energy efficiency, improve climate modeling, and support the transition toward more sustainable infrastructure and industries.

With a forward-thinking and environmentally grounded perspective, Silas examines applications ranging from smart grids and energy forecasting to climate risk analysis, carbon measurement, and resource optimization. He focuses on practical deployments where AI contributes measurable environmental benefits, while also addressing the limitations, trade-offs, and long-term implications of scaling these technologies responsibly.

news.title: Canva adds an AI ‘off’ button
news.title_en: Canva adds an AI ‘off’ button
news.author: Emma Roth
news.content_snippet:
Canva will now allow you to turn off its generative AI features. With this change, you can disable the graphic design platform’s array of AI tools, such as its AI photo-extending Magic Expand feature, as well as turn off the ability to generate images with its Canva chatbot.

news.summary_en: Canva has introduced an 'off' switch for generative AI features, allowing users to disable tools like Magic Expand and its chatbot while retaining non-generative utilities like background removal. This move responds to user frustration over AI proliferation and introduces filters to limit AI-generated content in search results.
paragraphs: Canva will now allow you to turn off its generative AI features. With this change, you can disable the graphic design platform’s array of AI tools, such as its AI photo-extending Magic Expand feature, as well as turn off the ability to generate images with its Canva chatbot.

This toggle doesn’t turn off every AI-powered feature on Canva, however. That includes Canva’s background remover and its Magic Grab tool, which lets you select an object in an image and move it somewhere else. “Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design,” Canva says.
The toggle still turns off many of Canva’s other AI features, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, AI Shapes, and more.

Since Canva’s big push into AI in 2023, some users have expressed frustration with the influx of AI features and asked for ways to turn them off. Canva has only continued to expand on its AI-powered image-editing suite since then, by rolling out a prompt-powered editing update in April and launching its first in-house AI model, Canva Craft, last month.

You can also now switch a toggle to see less AI content in Canva’s content library. Switching this option on means you’ll see human-created content first when searching through Canva’s library for templates, graphics, and other design elements. Canva says a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated content, and that any design that uses one of these elements will have an AI label in its metadata.

To turn off Canva’s AI features, head to Profile > Settings > Permission, and then toggle off Enable generative AI features. You can choose to see less AI-generated content by going to Profile > Your account > AI personalization, and then turning on the option to show less AI content. These switches are available to both free and paid users.

paragraphs: Dustin Moskovitz was one of Anthropic’s earliest investors, and that bet is expected to be worth billions as the company goes public Thursday.
The moment seems to fill him with worry.

The 42-year-old billionaire made his fortune as co-founder of Facebook and has, for years, been both intrigued and troubled by the path of artificial intelligence. He donated to OpenAI early on only to fall out with the company’s leaders as it became more of a business.

Anthropic was supposed to be different. Founded by Dario Amodei and other OpenAI employees who were concerned that A.I. wasn’t being developed for the good of humanity, Anthropic’s priority would be A.I. safety. Mr. Moskovitz helped get it off the ground.

Mr. Moskovitz embodies a tension between free-market capitalism and A.I. safety at the heart of Anthropic’s initial public offering. In multiple posts on social media, he has expressed his worry that Anthropic — and A.I. — is advancing too quickly for society to control, just as Wall Street hands Anthropic more than $80 billion of additional firepower in the biggest I.P.O. ever.
In a statement to The New York Times, Mr. Moskovitz established some distance from the company, where he served as a board observer, or a nonvoting board member.

“Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,” he said, referring to his wife, Cari Tuna. “A.I. is moving too fast. Anthropic and everyone else on the frontier should slow down and stop racing.”

In an unusual move, the couple transferred their Anthropic stake — which would be worth billions of dollars today — into a nonprofit in early 2025 so that he and Ms. Tuna would not personally profit from selling the stock in the public market, a spokesman for the couple said. The spokesman, Mike Levine, declined to disclose the nonprofit.

Mr. Moskovitz, who is one of the country’s biggest Democratic donors, is also deeply involved in the effective altruist movement. He is the biggest funder of nonprofits devoted to A.I. safety — often led by early A.I. believers who are disturbed that stock market expectations will overpower safety concerns for leading A.I. companies like Anthropic. They see the potential dangers multiplying as A.I. systems improve rapidly, pointing to recent episodes of so-called A.I. “agents” coordinating their own cyberattacks outside of controlled environments.

Mr. Moskovitz’s unease has estranged him from close friends in Silicon Valley, like the Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg, his former Harvard University roommate, and it has made him a foil for rivals like SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk, a frequent target of Mr. Moskovitz online.

Eric Ries, a former Anthropic adviser who helped the company set up a unique corporate structure, said the company had taken steps to insulate itself from some of the typical Wall Street pressures. But he knows his friend, Mr. Moskovitz, still worries.

“This is the one time when it’s been bad for someone to have invested early and called their shot and gotten it right,” said Mr. Ries, who advises Silicon Valley companies about management practices. Mr. Moskovitz, he added, appears to feel a sense of his place in history, which creates a “tremendous pressure and responsibility to get it right.”

Mr. Moskovitz, who declined to be interviewed for this article and makes few public appearances, has given the clearest expression of how he feels on the liberal-leaning social network Bluesky, where he gleefully debates his critics, offers candid anecdotes about and takedowns of fellow Silicon Valley titans, and occasionally discloses inside-the-boardroom information about Anthropic.
Mr. Moskovitz has christened himself an “ ‘overly online’ board observer.” Some of Mr. Moskovitz’s allies have been alarmed by his level of frankness on the platform.
In April, for instance, Mr. Moskovitz wrote that he felt Anthropic going public was “problematic” and that he had “tried to advise them to delay.”

By September, Mr. Moskovitz’s tone had turned sardonic. He recapped recent A.I. developments — cybersecurity failures, claims of potential human extinction, A.I. agents escaping sandboxes — landing on a dose of dark humor about the multitrillion-dollar valuation Anthropic could command when it starts publicly trading: “And one $2T IPO is proceeding as scheduled.”

Mr. Moskovitz and Dr. Amodei had known each other long before Anthropic’s founding. They were part of a social circle interested in effective altruism, the brainy, tech-inflected approach to philanthropy that uses data-driven evidence to inform decision-making.

They met through Holden Karnofsky, who helped create Open Philanthropy, Mr. Moskovitz’s effective-altruistic organization. Mr. Karnofsky was dating, and later married, Daniela Amodei, Dario’s sister. Dr. Amodei once joined Mr. Moskovitz at Burning Man, the desert festival popular with the tech crowd, according to a person who knows Mr. Moskovitz.

Dr. Amodei had just joined OpenAI, then a small San Francisco-based research lab that operated as a nonprofit when he helped arrange for Open Philanthropy, now called Coefficient Giving, to donate $30 million to OpenAI in 2017. Mr. Moskovitz said he saw the deal as a way to give Mr. Karnofsky a seat on its board and push the company in a safety direction. “If they have a bad approach now, that’s all the more reason to get involved,” Mr. Moskovitz wrote Mr. Karnofsky in late 2016, according to an email he has shared.
Mr. Moskovitz later said that strategy didn’t work — and that he was “most gullible” for backing OpenAI.

Over time, Dr. Amodei became more vocal inside OpenAI about the potential harms from A.I., and in 2020, he and his sister, who also worked at OpenAI, along with five of their colleagues, left the company to start Anthropic. They set it up as a for-profit company with an untypical legal structure — a public benefit corporation that would lessen the influence of outside shareholders.

The group struggled to win the backing of traditional venture capitalists, which it needed in the expensive business of developing A.I. models. Then Mr. Moskovitz came along. He invested $15 million to $25 million of the $124 million Anthropic raised overall in its first round of funding in 2021, according to two people familiar with the funding round.

Earlier this year, Mr. Moskovitz said in a post that his goal in funding the company was to extricate the founders from OpenAI and “create a race to the top (of ethics) by having a real safety lab at the frontier.” He added, without apparent irony, that his funding of Anthropic “might well be an action that ended the world.”

Mr. Moskovitz was one of the few people in Anthropic’s board room with extensive business credentials in the company’s early years. He had spent years running Asana, a workplace software company he founded, which had gone public in 2020, and was valued at roughly $25 billion at its height.

At times, he pressed executives on standard commercial issues, such as how they would get the company’s A.I. chatbot, Claude, into the hands of more corporate customers, a person close to Anthropic said.
Other times, he asked for specific plans about the security and safety of its models, said a person who attended one of those board meetings.

Meanwhile, Mr. Moskovitz was putting more and more money into A.I. safety projects, through both effective altruism and Democratic politics. Mr. Moskovitz and Ms. Tuna have donated over $8 billion to charity. In April, Mr. Moskovitz said he had committed about $20 billion more to charitable efforts, which includes the Anthropic stake. Most of the couple’s funding has gone toward global-health efforts like disease prevention, as well as to A.I. safety nonprofits.

And over the last decade, Mr. Moskovitz has achieved first-name-only-required status in Democratic circles, meeting privately with President Joseph Biden Jr. to talk about A.I. safety and donating about $140 million to liberal super PACs.

That has put him at odds with tech billionaires who have increasingly made a rightward tilt. Mr. Moskovitz has squabbled online with Marc Andreessen, who serves on the board of Meta and was one of Asana’s first investors and who has allied himself with the Trump administration’s freewheeling position on A.I. development.

Mr. Moskovitz has at times been consumed with blasting Mr. Musk and Tesla, which he once called an Enron-like fraud. Not to be outdone, Mr. Musk retorted on social media that Mr. Moskovitz was “a pompous idiot.”
Mr. Moskovitz wrote and shared a five-page memo about why effective altruists should not work with Mr. Musk. One section, according to a Bluesky post, was titled “Elon is a Bad Person.”

Perhaps the most telling sign of Mr. Moskovitz’s disappointments with Silicon Valley has been the recent, surprising change of tone around the company that made him a billionaire in the first place: Facebook.

Mr. Moskovitz has long defended the company and Mr. Zuckerberg even as he excoriated the Valley. But in the last year, Mr. Moskovitz has sharply critiqued Mr. Zuckerberg and Meta, primarily for creating addiction and spreading misinformation ever since their decision to start News Feed, what he called the company’s “original sin.”

“I absolutely made these cases of harm to Zuck and other execs, many times,” he wrote in April. “I am very sorry for failing to stop the madness and every day I’m embarrassed to have helped it begin.”
Mr. Moskovitz wrote in May that he sold all of his remaining stake in the company and he did so “precisely because I don’t approve of the company’s actions.”
Mr. Zuckerberg is similarly privately frustrated with Mr. Moskovitz and his point of view on A.I., according to a person who has spoken to Mr. Zuckerberg about it.

After leaving Facebook, Mr. Moskovitz struggled at Asana with short-term shareholder pressures. As its stock price slid, he used his own money to buy shares and prove he still had faith in the company.
Mr. Moskovitz stepped down as Asana’s chief executive last year. Its market capitalization has fallen to about $2 billion.

Mr. Ries, who advised Mr. Moskovitz at Asana, said he thought the experience as a public company chief executive helped shape his views on Anthropic’s I.P.O. “He knows first hand the ways that markets puts pressure on mission-driven companies, ” Mr. Ries added, referring to Asana. “He’s seen this financial gravity up close and it hasn’t been pretty.”

In the run-up to the public offering, Mr. Moskovitz has expressed frustration that no one — not at Anthropic, not in politics — seems to be listening to him. Neither Dario nor Daniela Amodei has spoken to Mr. Moskovitz in over a year, said a person with knowledge of their conversations.

He said he no longer speaks to his once “close friends” Mr. Zuckerberg or Sam Altman, the OpenAI chief executive. Even Mr. Karnofsky, his longtime top aide who in 2024 left Open Philanthropy and now works at Anthropic in a technical role, basically does not have time for some of his complaints, Mr. Moskovitz wrote on Bluesky.
“What policymakers and politicians are listening to me? Where are they? I want to finally meet one,” he wrote last year. “Attempting to be heard is not the same as being listened to.”

[Context & Motivation] Yesterday, while we were all waiting for Anthropic's IPO to price (more on that below), our colleagues reported ….
[Key Metrics] Situational Awareness has a $5bn stake in Anthropic — and Aschenbrenner’s wife is chief of staff to its CEO Dario Amodei.
paragraphs: This article is an on-site version of our Unhedged newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every weekday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here, or explore all FT newsletters

Good morning. Yesterday, while we were all waiting for Anthropic’s IPO to price (more on that below), our colleagues reported that Leopold Aschenbrenner of Situational Awareness was scheming to reboot the hedge fund after its spectacular meltdown in July. The timing of this attempt with the huge IPO may not be a coincidence. Situational Awareness has a $5bn stake in Anthropic — and Aschenbrenner’s wife is chief of staff to its CEO Dario Amodei. It’s a small world, after all. Send us your thoughts: [email protected].

It is IPO day for Anthropic, and the shares have priced at $83, valuing the company at $1.5tn. This newsletter is therefore obliged to add a few drops to the roaring river of ink already poured out on the topic of whether the company can be worth so much.

We haven’t the slightest idea how to answer this question with any rigour, and we don’t think anyone else does either. So we will change the topic slightly and ask: what will Anthropic have to do over the medium to long term — the next five to 10 years, say — in order to be considered a financial success? Specifically, how much revenue does it need to earn?

Start with return on invested capital (which is operating profit after tax/capital invested). Anthropic has approximately $901bn in off-balance-sheet financial commitments, “substantially all of which is related to [buying] compute and infrastructure” (that’s from the S-1, page 173), plus another set of commitments the exact dollar value of which is “not yet determinable”, but that the company estimates at $150bn to $175bn. So let’s call it an even trillion. The commitments are spread out over the next 15 years or so, but $700bn comes due in the next five, reckons the Zion Research Group, which specialises in accounting research.

Let’s suppose, generously, that this trillion is all the capital that is going to sit inside the business. What sort of return will investors expect on that? I think something like 20 per cent is fair. This is the neighbourhood of other tech mega-companies. Five-year average ROIC at Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Microsoft are 19, 43, 19 and 20 per cent, respectively, according to S&P Capital IQ. Twenty per cent ROIC implies $200bn a year in operating profit after tax.

Proceeding in this same gestural but hopefully not insane fashion, assume an operating margin of 40 per cent (that same cohort of peers comes in at 30, 31, 37 and 44 per cent, respectively), and an effective tax rate of 17 per cent (same drill: 16, 17, 19 and 17). All that together implies a revenue run-rate of $602bn a year (ie, {200/[1-.17]}/.4).
(Don’t like my calculation? By all means, email me yours.)

This is a big number — even if some Wall Street analysts have pencilled in an even bigger one for 2030. For comparison: current annual revenue at Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Microsoft is $471bn, $478bn, $241bn and $346bn, respectively. Alternatively, you could compare the number to the entire software and IT services sector of the S&P 1500 index (which captures almost all large-, mid- and small-cap US stocks): 76 companies with $908bn in revenue.
So, if you plan to buy the IPO and hold it, you just need to answer a simple question, put to me by Richard Kramer of Arete Research: where is all that revenue going to come from?
The Jensen Huang, er, affair has drawn renewed attention to semiconductor export controls. Until last week, Nvidia and Anthropic represented competing poles in that debate.
Huang, Nvidia’s former chief executive, was the AI industry’s loudest opponent of restrictions on chip sales to China. In April, he told the Dwarkesh Podcast:
“. . . of course we’re going to send them compute. So what? The fact of the matter is that we get the benefit. Don’t forget, we get the benefit of American technology leadership.”
. . . of course we’re going to send them compute. So what? The fact of the matter is that we get the benefit. Don’t forget, we get the benefit of American technology leadership.

Huang was, of course, motivated to argue for greater market access for his company. The short seller Culpepper Research estimated in May that more than a fifth of Nvidia’s computing revenue was driven by demand from China, despite US export restrictions.
Huang wants to be a free trader and national security hawk at the same time. He told the Dwarkesh Podcast:
“To concede that market [China] for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country. It is a disservice to our national security. It is a disservice to our technology leadership”
To concede that market [China] for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country. It is a disservice to our national security. It is a disservice to our technology leadership

Anthropic’s chief executive, Amodei, has spent years arguing for restrictions on China’s access to Nvidia’s most powerful chips. According to Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles, Amodei and co-founder Jack Clark were advocating for export controls as early as 2021. But, again, this is a position Amodei is motivated to take. Export controls hobble his Chinese competition.

The difference in views is striking because Nvidia is one of Anthropic’s financial backers. It invested in the AI model maker earlier this year and committed to buying $10bn of the stock at the IPO price today.

Huang’s fall may prove to be Amodei’s gain. Nvidia said on Tuesday that it would stop selling advanced chips to China and established a committee to oversee national security and trade compliance. Meanwhile, the US is moving to close the loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access those chips by renting computing power from data centres in south-east Asia and Brazil. The upshot is Nvidia may find itself selling fewer chips to Asia and more to Anthropic. Two-nil to Amodei.

news.summary_en: German Media Minister Wolfram Weimer and Austrian Digital Secretary Alexander Pröll have proposed moving TikTok's European operations under European ownership. The initiative aims to mitigate data security concerns related to its Chinese parent company, ByteDance, mirroring recent forced-divestiture models seen in the US.
paragraphs: Germany and Austria want TikTok’s European business to come under European ownership. Ministers from both countries made the call in a joint statement on Wednesday, POLITICO reported.

Germany’s media minister Wolfram Weimer and Austria’s state secretary for digitalisation Alexander Pröll said the move would keep personal data safe and give Europe more control. They called TikTok a threat to democracy.
The problem starts with TikTok’s Chinese owner ByteDance, the ministers said. They fear the Chinese state can get at the data of millions of Europeans.
TikTok has about 200 million users in the EU, according to the statement. The ministers called on other EU countries to join them, but did not say how a new owner would be found.
TikTok rejected the idea, POLITICO reported.
A TikTok spokesperson said there was “” to the proposal.
The plan follows the US model. In January, TikTok’s US business moved into a new joint venture led by Oracle, Silver Lake and MGX. ByteDance kept a stake of nearly 20%.
Weimer first pushed the idea in May. At the time, the European Commission said it looks at compliance with EU rules, not at who owns a company.
TikTok is already under pressure in Europe. Ireland’s data regulator fined TikTok €530m in 2025 over transfers of European user data to China. The EU is also looking into its role in elections.
EU culture ministers meet in Brussels on Thursday.

news.title_en: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
news.author: Antonio Regalado
news.summary_en:

paragraphs: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days —the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins , the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs , a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “ organ medicine” : research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

news.title: Google is forcing Android app developers to properly support foldables
news.title_en: Google is forcing Android app developers to properly support foldables
news.author: Jay Peters
news.summary_en:
Now that Apple’s foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. paragraphs: Now that Apple’s foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. If they don’t, developers risk not being able to publish or update their apps or have reduced visibility for their apps on Google Play.

Google says Android apps must meet its “Tier 3 — Adaptive ready” standard. “Apps must fill the available display area without letterboxing or compatibility modes,” Google says. “Apps must preserve state (scroll position, text input, media playback) during rotation, folding/unfolding, and resizing, while supporting multi-window environments.” (The other two tiers are “Adaptive optimized” and “Adaptive differentiated” and take further advantage of the possibilities of foldables.) As of the April 2027 deadline, developers also will have to include three foldable screenshots for their app listings. Developers can start publishing their foldable screenshots today.

Similar requirements will apply to games, though developers have until August 2027 to get their titles ready for Android foldables, Google says. (Google “plans to extend” its requirements to other large-screen devices like tablets and Googlebook laptops in “future phases.”) However, game developers will still need to share three foldable screenshots for app listings starting in April.

The changes are being announced just weeks after Apple launched the iPhone Duo, which already has more than 200,000 optimized apps, though some developers are still figuring out Apple’s foldable form factor.

paragraphs: Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.

The company is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself.

The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the company is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat.
Developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month.

Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance.
With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters.

AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says.

The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The company notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time.
Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

paragraphs: Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in seven weeks. Neon is nearly twice as fast as its sibling Carbon, beats it on most benchmarks and costs significantly less. Google continues to ship at a remarkable pace.

Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, already its fourth AI model in seven weeks. Neon offers a one-million-token context window for text, images, audio and video, and Google positions it between Carbon and Hydrogen.

At its highest reasoning level, "xhigh,"Neon scores 61 points on the Intelligence Index, edging past Gemini 4 Carbon at 60 points and landing in third place behind OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2, both of which Google omits from its own comparison table.
### The Cost Advantage Comes from List Price, Not Token Efficiency

Through Google AI Studio and Gemini for Business, one million input tokens costs three dollars (or $0.15 when cached) and one million output tokens costs fifteen dollars. That is 25 percent below Carbon's regular price of four and twenty dollars, but 50 percent above Carbon's promotional price, which remains in effect through the end of November.

According to Artificial Analysis, per-task costs for Neon at xhigh come in at $6.44, roughly 17 percent below Carbon's undiscounted figure of $7.76. Neon actually uses about 15 percent more output tokens per task than Carbon, so the savings come entirely from the lower per-token list price. At the second-highest level, "high,"Neon matches Carbon's intelligence score while cutting per-task costs in half. Processing time for the benchmark also drops from about 36 minutes to roughly 21 minutes because Neon generates around 110 tokens per second, nearly double Carbon's rate of 57 tokens per second.
### Half the Cost for Coding Agents and Strong Visual Analysis

The model is especially competitive on the Coding Agent Index. Inside Google Antigravity, Neon at xhigh scores 59 points, beating Carbon (55 points) as well as Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 (58 points each) at a fraction of the price. An average coding task costs $6.86 with Neon, compared to $12.61 for Opus and $15.47 for Fable. In the SWE-sweep test, the Antigravity environment triples Neon's hit rate to 39.0 percent, according to Google.

Artificial Analysis measured large gains in visual processing. On the document test GDP.pdf, Neon at "high"hits the top score of 33.4 percent, five points ahead of Carbon, though it oddly falls back to 28.0 percent at "xhigh."On the AA-Briefcase test, Neon takes the lead for best presentation quality with 1771 Elo points, ahead of Opus 5.5.

In Google's own evaluations, Neon also leads individual categories on the Vals Index, Zapier's AutomationBench (56.3 percent) and science tests such as RiemannBench (84.0 percent). For security professionals, Google is launching a cyber variant through the Fairwind Program that delivers top scores on SEC-bench Pro (90.5 percent) and WebExploitBench v1.2 (51.26 percent) at half the price of competing models. According to Neon's (very brief) Model Card, the model blocks 100 percent of indirect prompt-injection attacks on the Gray-Swan benchmark.

news.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
news.title_en: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
news.author: WIRED
news.summary_en:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified n
paragraphs: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
### 1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
### 2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
### 3. Check trusted sources of network data

When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon —but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she says.
### 4. Look for claims of responsibility

Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.
### 5. Sit tight and reserve judgment

If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”

Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”
In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.

“If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”
This story originally appeared on wired.com.
subheadings: 1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence
2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved
3. Check trusted sources of network data
4. Look for claims of responsibility
5. Sit tight and reserve judgment

paragraphs: Todd Underwood, a former Anthropic engineering leader, fielded a stream of calls in recent months from investment managers eager to gain his insider view on the artificial intelligence giant’s business strategy ahead of this week’s initial public offering.
But few of the questions focused on an aspect of the company Mr. Underwood viewed as a crucial asset: Anthropic’s unusual governance structure.

The company is set to become by far the most valuable company on the stock market with the legal designation of a public benefit corporation, or P.B.C. That status requires Anthropic to prioritize its corporate mission — to develop safe A.I. systems “for the long-term benefit of humanity” — in addition to the customary sole focus on value for stockholders.
The company’s public benefit mandate is guarded partly by a five-member “long-term benefit trust,” which includes Ben Bernanke, the former Federal Reserve chair.

The company “will choose to do things in favor of safety rather than in favor of making money,” said Mr. Underwood, who has been sought out by investors as a former employee for insights into the company. He added that he agreed with that focus but thought it might turn off some investors.
The company’s public offering sets up an important test as Anthropic goes from one of the most closely watched private companies in the world to one of the most scrutinized.

Anthropic is expected to spend its first two years as a publicly traded company asking investors for patience as it burns hundreds of billions of dollars of cash to invest in new chips and data centers. It is also facing increasing calls from A.I. safety advocates, as well as some of its own employees, to slow down its pace of training new models.

On Wednesday, the company is expected to sell roughly $65 billion in shares, making it the second-largest I.P.O. after SpaceX’s earlier this year. It also has $26 billion of investments lined up from tech giants like Nvidia and Microsoft.

Anthropic’s expected market capitalization, more than $1.4 trillion, would make it 30 times as valuable as the next public benefit corporation that trades on the stock market, the software maker Veeva Systems.

Anthropic was founded as a public benefit corporation in 2021, and formed its long-term benefit trust in 2023 as a way to give the structure teeth, ensuring the company balances goals for shareholders and its broader mission. The structure is taxed the same as any corporation.

The trust is made up of a group of “financially disinterested” experts in economics, science and global health who don’t own Anthropic stock, the company said in its offering prospectus. The group has the power to appoint and remove several of the company’s board members, authority that is typically given only to shareholders.

Adding to the unusual leadership structure, the company also spent the months leading up to its public offering locking in new authority for the executives who started the company nearly six years ago, according to securities filings.

The company created a new class of shares this fall for its unusually large co-founding team — seven executives, including the chief executive, Dario Amodei — that give them 50.1 percent of voting control over the company, collectively. The founders have the ability to appoint other board members.

A founder-controlled board committee can also help overrule one of the trust’s four board appointments, reducing the trust’s power, said Jesse M. Fried, a Harvard law professor who has studied Anthropic’s corporate structure.
The trust’s authority was “watered down” as a result of the changes, but they don’t “fundamentally change the governance of the company,” he added.
Anthropic’s structure is unique when compared with other publicly traded companies, corporate governance experts said.

“I don’t know if I can really compare it to anything else,” said Douglas Chia, a senior fellow at Rutgers Law School who advises companies on corporate governance. “It’s going to be an interesting experiment.”

The Council of Institutional Investors, an advocacy group that represents public, union and corporate pension funds, has long been critical of arrangements that give founders voting control disproportionate to their financial stakes. The group wrote a letter this year expressing concerns that when SpaceX went public, it gave its founder, Elon Musk, dominant voting control.

The group will “wait and see” how Anthropic’s structure plays out, said Glenn Davis, the council’s executive director. The founders’ immense voting power means that “ultimately the founders are accountable to themselves,” rather than shareholders, he added.

The layered structure could still challenge investors’ understanding of the company and the group of people who govern it, said Paul Abrahimzadeh, a senior partner at the tech investment firm 1789 Capital.
Still, investor enthusiasm was inevitable despite the uncertainties, he added. “You have to own it. The question is at what price?”

paragraphs: Published on 11/19/2026 at 05:44 am EST
Alibaba Group recorded a surge in fiscal second-quarter profit as its AI profitability and e-commerce business improved.

The Hangzhou-based company has doubled down on artificial intelligence as a growth driver, a push that faces a new risk from heightened scrutiny about exports of chips to China. It has committed to spending more than $53 billion over three years to develop both the hardware and software that power AI.

Its success on that front holds the key to staying competitive amid challenges from other big tech firms and startups alike. But going all in on AI has proved a drag on profitability over recent quarters, putting pressure on Alibaba to deliver on its AI goals.
Its latest results look reassuring.

On Thursday, Alibaba said net profit tripled from a year earlier to 64.535 billion yuan, equivalent to $9.68 billion, for the three months ended September. Analysts polled by FactSet had expected 23.72 billion yuan. Revenue grew about 10% to 271.52 billion yuan, also better than market estimates.
Alibaba attributed the sharp profit improvement to higher net investment income and income from operations.

The earnings beat comes as Alibaba prepares a Hong Kong listing for its chip unit, T-Head, that investors view as a major validation of its efforts to produce in-house semiconductors. The business could fetch a valuation of $85 billion, according to Nomura estimates.

news.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
news.title_en: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
news.author: Casey Crownhart
news.summary_en:
After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

paragraphs: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

news.content_snippet:
Korea surpassed $1 trillion in annual exports for the first time Thursday, reaching the milestone at 2:09:38 p.m. as global AI investment boosted demand for semiconductors. It became the fourth country to reach the mark, after the United States, Germany and China. The government projects exports will total about $1.17 trillion this year, but officials warned that AI investment slowdowns, chip-price volatility and trade barriers could threaten momentum.
